sections.history: Keezhvelur, whose historical name is Thirukeezhvelur, is an ancient Shaiva site near Nagapattinam, revered in the seventh-century Tevaram by both Sambandar and Appar. The temple is a Maadakovil — one of the raised temples traditionally attributed to the early Chola king Kochengat Chola, built high so that an elephant could not enter the sanctum. The present fabric, altered and renovated over centuries, is held to be at least a thousand years old; its antiquity rests on its Tevaram standing and its sculptures.
sections.architecture: As a Maadakovil, the temple sits on an elevated base, its sanctum reached by a flight of steps — a form distinctive to the Kochengat Chola foundations. The east-facing rajagopuram rises seven tiers, with the Saravana Theertham opposite. The sanctum enshrines Kediliappar, Akshayalingeswarar, and the goddess Vanamulai Amman has her own shrine. The temple's Nataraja is shown with the right foot raised, a rare posture said to be the form the lord revealed to the sage Agastya.
sections.legends: The sthala-purana traces the temple to the churning of the ocean of milk: a drop of the amrita, the nectar of immortality, is said to have fallen here and grown into a forest of ilanthai, the jujube, which became the temple's sacred tree. The raised Maadakovil form is explained by the devotion of Kochengat Chola, who in tradition built such temples so tall that elephants could not disturb the worship. The right-foot-raised Nataraja recalls the grace shown to Agastya, for whom the lord reversed his dancing posture.
sections.festivals: The temple keeps the Shaiva festival calendar — Maha Shivaratri, Pradosham, the Margazhi observances and the annual Brahmotsavam — with Arudra Darshan honouring the special Nataraja held in particular regard. The elevated sanctum gives the festival processions and the climb to darshan a distinctive character.
sections.experience: Climbing to the raised sanctum of a Maadakovil is itself part of the pilgrimage at Keezhvelur, lifting the devotee above the surrounding fields toward the lord. The seven-tiered tower, the jujube tree of the nectar legend and the rare right-footed Nataraja give the temple a quiet distinction, and the darshan of Kediliappar — the 'faultless lord' — carries a sense of completeness and grace.

visit.timings: Typically open from early morning to midday and again from late afternoon into the evening; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected, with shoulders and knees covered; footwear is left at the entrance.
visit.photography: Photography is generally allowed in the outer corridors but not inside the sanctum; ask temple staff before photographing rituals.
visit.gettingThere: Keezhvelur is in Nagapattinam district, about 10 km from Nagapattinam and near Tiruvarur; the nearest rail heads are Nagapattinam and Tiruvarur, with local buses and taxis to the town.
